items.text: We propose SPECTER, a new method to generate document-level embedding of scientiﬁc documents based on pretraining a Transformer language model on a powerful signal of document-level relatedness: the citation graph.
items.why: Defines core method.
items.plain: We introduce SPECTER, which creates scientific document embeddings by pretraining a Transformer language model using citation links.

items.text: Unlike existing pretrained language models, SPECTER can be easily applied to downstream applications without task-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning.
items.why: States major operational assumption/advantage.
items.plain: SPECTER can be used in downstream applications as-is, without needing task-specific fine-tuning.

items.text: Additionally, to encourage further research on document-level models, we introduce SCIDOCS, a new evaluation benchmark consisting of seven document-level tasks ranging from citation prediction, to document classiﬁcation and recommendation.
items.why: Introduces evaluation benchmark.
items.plain: We introduce SCIDOCS, a benchmark with seven document-level tasks including citation prediction, document classification, and recommendation.

items.text: Our system, SPECTER,2 incorporates inter-document context into the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) language models (e.g., SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019)) to learn document representations that are effective across a wide-variety of downstream tasks, without the need for any task-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning of the pretrained language model.
items.why: Explains base architecture and feature-based usage.
items.plain: SPECTER adds multi-document context into Transformer language models like SciBERT to generate effective document embeddings without task-specific fine-tuning.

items.text: We speciﬁcally use citations as a naturally occurring, inter-document incidental supervision signal indicating which documents are most related and formulate the signal into a triplet-loss pretraining objective.
items.why: Defines the core supervision signal and loss formulation.
items.plain: We use citations as a natural signal of document similarity and train the model using a triplet loss objective.

items.text: Unlike many prior works, at inference time, our model does not require any citation information.
items.why: Clarifies input requirements at inference time.
items.plain: During inference, our model does not require citation information.

items.text: With respect to the terminology used by Devlin et al. (2019), unlike most existing LMs that are “ﬁne-tuning based”, our approach results in embeddings that can be applied to downstream tasks in a “feature-based” fashion, meaning the learned paper embeddings can be easily used as features, with no need for further task-speciﬁc ﬁne-tuning.
items.why: Distinguishes feature-based approach from fine-tuning.
items.plain: Our model produces embeddings used as fixed features in downstream tasks, rather than requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

items.text: Speciﬁcally, we use SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019) which is an adaptation of the original BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) architecture to the scientiﬁc domain.
items.why: Specifies foundational language model.
items.plain: We build SPECTER using SciBERT, a BERT model adapted for scientific text.

items.text: SPECTER builds embeddings from the title and abstract of a paper.
items.why: States exact text fields used as input.
items.plain: SPECTER creates embeddings using only a paper's title and abstract.

items.text: As such, we encode the concatenated title and abstract using a Transformer LM (e.g., SciBERT) and take the ﬁnal representation of the [CLS] token as the output representation of the paper:5
items.why: Defines how document vector is extracted.
items.plain: We pass the concatenated title and abstract through a Transformer language model and use the final [CLS] token representation as the paper's vector embedding.

items.text: In particular, each training instance is a triplet of papers: a query paper PQ, a positive paper P+ and a negative paper P−.
items.why: Defines the training data structure.
items.plain: Each training sample is a triplet made of a query paper, a cited positive paper, and an uncited negative paper.

items.text: The positive paper is a paper that the query paper cites, and the negative paper is a paper that is not cited by the query paper (but that may be cited by P+).
items.why: Defines positive and negative selection criteria.
items.plain: The positive paper is cited by the query paper, while the negative paper is not cited by the query paper.

items.text: We then train the model using the following triplet margin loss function:
items.why: Identifies objective function type.
items.plain: We train the model using a triplet margin loss function.

items.text: where d is a distance function and m is the loss margin hyperparameter (we empirically choose m = 1).
items.why: Specifies chosen hyperparameter value.
items.plain: In the loss function, d represents distance and m is the loss margin, set to 1 based on experiments.

items.text: We consider two sets of negative examples: the ﬁrst set simply consists of randomly selected papers from the corpus.
items.why: Describes first category of negative samples.
items.plain: The first set of negative examples consists of randomly selected papers from the corpus.

items.text: We denote as “hard negatives” the papers that are not cited by the
items.why: Defines 'hard negative' distractors.
items.plain: Hard negatives are papers not cited by the query paper, but cited by one of its cited papers.

items.text: At inference time, the model receives one paper, P, and it outputs the SPECTER’s Transfomer pooled output activation as the paper representation for P (Equation 1).
items.why: Details inference setup.
items.plain: At inference time, the model takes one paper and outputs its pooled Transformer activation as the paper embedding.

items.text: We note that for inference, SPECTER requires only the title and abstract of the given input paper; the model does not need any citation information about the input paper.
items.why: Confirms missing-data behavior at test time.
items.plain: SPECTER only needs the title and abstract to run inference, requiring no citation data.

items.text: Note that SPECTER will not be further ﬁne-tuned on any of the tasks; we simply plug in the embeddings as features for each task.
items.why: States evaluation rule for SPECTER on benchmark tasks.
items.plain: SPECTER is not fine-tuned on benchmark tasks; its embeddings are used directly as features.

items.text: We construct a dataset consisting of 23K academic
items.why: Details MeSH classification dataset size.
items.plain: The MeSH dataset contains 23,000 academic medical papers split across 11 disease classes.

items.text: For our evaluation, we derive a document classiﬁcation dataset from the level 1 topics, where a paper is labeled by its corresponding level 1 MAG topic.
items.why: Details MAG topic classification dataset setup.
items.plain: We created a document classification dataset of 25,000 papers evenly split across 19 level-1 topic categories.

items.text: The evaluation dataset includes approximately 30K total papers from a held-out pool of papers, consisting of 1K query papers and a candidate set of up to 5 cited papers and 25 (randomly selected) uncited papers.
items.why: Describes experimental setup for direct citation prediction.
items.plain: The direct citation task uses 30,000 papers, where 1,000 query papers must rank up to 5 cited candidate papers above 25 random uncited papers.

items.text: For each embedding method, we require only comparing the L2 distance between the raw embeddings of the query and the candidates, without any additional trainable parameters.
items.why: Explains ranking evaluation metric calculation without parameters.
items.plain: Embeddings are evaluated by comparing L2 distances between query and candidate vectors, with no additional trainable parameters.

items.text: Co-Views Our co-views dataset consists of approximately 30K papers.
items.why: Describes Co-Views dataset size and construction.
items.plain: The co-views dataset includes about 30,000 papers evaluated using 1,000 query papers matched with co-viewed and random candidates.

items.text: We use a dataset of user clickthrough data for this task which consists of 22K clickthrough events from a public scholarly search engine.
items.why: Describes recommendation task dataset size.
items.plain: The recommendation dataset contains 22,000 clickthrough events split into 20,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 1,000 test examples.

items.text: by dividing the score for each test example by the propensity score for the clicked position.
items.why: Details debiasing procedure for click metrics.
items.plain: Evaluation scores are debiased by dividing each test example's score by the propensity score of its clicked position.

items.text: We test different embeddings on the recommendation task by including cosine embedding distance9 as a feature within an existing recommendation system that includes several other informative features (title/author similarity, reference and citation overlap, etc.).
items.why: Explains how embeddings enter recommendation pipeline.
items.plain: Embedding cosine distance is added as one feature alongside title, author, and citation features in an existing recommender system.

items.text: Training Data To train our model, we use a subset of the Semantic Scholar corpus (Ammar et al., 2018) consisting of about 146K query papers (around 26.7M tokens) with their corresponding outgoing citations, and we use an additional 32K papers for validation.
items.why: Provides training dataset source and scale.
items.plain: The training set uses around 146,000 query papers from Semantic Scholar, with 32,000 papers kept for validation.

items.text: We empirically found it helpful to use 2 hard negatives (citations of citations) and 3 easy negatives (randomly selected papers) for each query paper.
items.why: Specifies precise ratio of hard and easy negatives.
items.plain: Each query paper uses 2 hard negatives (citations of citations) and 3 easy negatives (random papers).

items.text: This process results in about 684K training triples and 145K validation triples.
items.why: Reports exact triplet training count.
items.plain: This setup yields roughly 684,000 training triplets and 145,000 validation triplets.

items.text: We initialize the model from SciBERT pretrained weights (Beltagy et al., 2019) since it is the stateof-the-art pretrained language model on scientiﬁc text.
items.why: Notes weight initialization baseline.
items.plain: The model initializes using pretrained weights from SciBERT.

items.text: We continue training all model parameters on our training objective (Equation 2).
items.why: Clarifies parameter update during pretraining.
items.plain: All model parameters are updated while training on the citation triplet loss.

items.text: For training, we use the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2014) following the suggested hyperparameters in Devlin et al. (2019) (LR: 2e-5, Slanted Triangular LR scheduler10 (Howard and Ruder, 2018) with number of train steps equal to training instances and cut fraction of 0.1).
items.why: Details optimizer and learning rate schedule.
items.plain: The model is trained using Adam with a 2e-5 learning rate and a linear warmup-decay scheduler.

items.text: We train the model on a single Titan V GPU (12G memory) for 2 epochs, with batch size of 4 (the maximum that ﬁt in our GPU memory) and use gradient accumulation for an effective batch size of 32.
items.why: Specifies hardware and effective batch size.
items.plain: Training uses a single Titan V GPU for 2 epochs with a batch size of 4 and gradient accumulation up to an effective batch size of 32.

items.text: Task-Speciﬁc Model Details For the classiﬁcation tasks, we used a linear SVM where embedding vectors were the only features.
items.why: Specifies classifier model used on top of embeddings.
items.plain: Classification tasks use a linear Support Vector Machine taking raw embedding vectors as input.

items.text: For the recommendation tasks, we use a feedforward ranking neural network that takes as input ten features designed to capture the similarity between each query and candidate paper, including the cosine similarity between the query and candidate embeddings and manually-designed features computed from the papers’ citations, titles, authors, and publication dates.
items.why: Describes model used for recommendation ranking task.
items.plain: The recommendation task uses a feedforward neural network that ranks papers using ten similarity features, including embedding cosine distance.

items.text: Overall, we observe substantial improvements across all tasks with average performance of 80.0 across all metrics on all tasks which is a 3.1 point absolute improvement over the next-best baseline.
items.why: Reports overall main result on SCIDOCS benchmark.
items.plain: SPECTER scores an overall average of 80.0 across all benchmark metrics, outperforming the next-best baseline by 3.1 points.

items.text: Particularly, on the MeSH (MAG) dataset, we obtain an 86.4 (82.0) F1 score which is about a ∆= + 2.3 (+1.5) point absolute increase over the best baseline on each dataset respectively.
items.why: Reports specific document classification improvement.
items.plain: SPECTER obtains an F1 score of 86.4 on MeSH and 82.0 on MAG, outperforming the best baselines by 2.3 and 1.5 points.

items.text: SPECTER achieves a MAP score of 83.8 on the co-view task, and 84.5 on coread, improving over the best baseline (Citeomatic in this case) by 2.7 and 4.0 points, respectively.
items.why: Reports key user activity prediction results.
items.plain: SPECTER achieves mean average precision scores of 83.8 on co-views and 84.5 on co-reads, beating the best baseline by 2.7 and 4.0 points.

items.text: On the other hand, on cocitation data our method is able to achieve the best results with nDCG of 94.8, improving over SGC with 2.3 points.
items.why: Reports co-citation result relative to graph baseline.
items.plain: SPECTER achieves a 94.8 normalized discounted cumulative gain on co-citation prediction, improving over the SGC model by 2.3 points.

items.text: Finally, for recommendation task, we observe that SPECTER outperforms all other models on this task as well, with nDCG of 53.9.
items.why: Reports offline recommendation metric.
items.plain: SPECTER achieves a 53.9 normalized discounted cumulative gain on the recommendation task, beating all baselines.

items.text: In a dataset of 4,113 clicks, we found that SPECTER ranker improved clickthrough rate over the baseline by 46.5%, demonstrating its superiority.
items.why: Reports live online A/B testing evidence.
items.plain: An online A/B test across 4,113 clicks showed that SPECTER increased recommendation clickthrough rates by 46.5% over the baseline.

items.text: We emphasize that our citation-based pretraining objective is critical for the performance of SPECTER; removing this and using a vanilla SciB- ERT results in decreased performance on all tasks.
items.why: States ablation result regarding citation pretraining.
items.plain: Removing the citation-based pretraining objective and using plain SciBERT degrades performance across all tasks.

items.text: We observe that removing the abstract from the textual input and relying only on the title results in a substantial decrease in performance.
items.why: Shows impact of removing abstract field.
items.plain: Using only the title without the abstract significantly reduces performance.

items.text: More surprisingly, adding authors as an input (along with title and abstract) hurts performance.13 One possible explanation is that author names are sparse in the corpus, making it difﬁcult for the model to infer document-level relatedness from them.
items.why: Shows counterintuitive result of adding author names.
items.plain: Adding author names alongside the title and abstract reduces model performance.

items.text: 13We experimented with both concatenating authors with the title and abstract and also considering them as an additional ﬁeld.
items.why: Specifies author metadata incorporation methods tested.
items.plain: Authors were evaluated both by concatenating them with titles/abstracts and by feeding them as a distinct field.

items.why: Provides exact numerical ablation results.
items.plain: Full SPECTER scores 80.0 overall, falling to 68.1 without abstracts, 79.9 with venue data, 67.3 with author data, 78.4 without hard negatives, and 77.5 starting from BERT-Large.

items.text: The ﬁfth row of Table 2 shows that this is important—using only easy negatives reduces performance on all tasks.
items.why: Confirms contribution of hard negative sampling.
items.plain: Removing hard negatives and relying only on easy random negatives lowers scores across all tasks.

items.text: The sixth row of the table shows that using a strong general-domain language model (BERT-Large) instead of SciBERT in SPECTER reduces performance considerably.
items.why: Demonstrates benefit of SciBERT initialization over BERT-Large.
items.plain: Starting SPECTER with BERT-Large instead of SciBERT noticeably reduces performance.

items.text: We experiment with ﬁne-tuning SciBERT on our tasks, and ﬁnd this to be generally inferior to using our ﬁxed representations from SPECTER.
items.why: Compares fixed representations against direct task fine-tuning.
items.plain: Fine-tuning SciBERT directly on downstream tasks produces worse overall performance than using SPECTER's fixed representations.

items.text: SPECTER 84.2 88.4 91.5 36.9 80.0 SciBERT ﬁne-tune on co-view 83.0 84.2 84.1 36.4 76.0 SciBERT ﬁne-tune on co-read 82.3 85.4 86.7 36.3 77.1 SciBERT ﬁne-tune on co-citation 82.9 84.3 85.2 36.6 76.4 SciBERT ﬁne-tune on multitask 83.3 86.1 88.2 36.0 78.0
items.why: Provides numerical evidence comparing SPECTER against task fine-tuning.
items.plain: SPECTER achieves an overall score of 80.0, compared to task-fine-tuned SciBERT scoring 76.0 on co-views, 77.1 on co-reads, 76.4 on co-citations, and 78.0 on multitask training.

items.text: We trained our own 300 dimensional fasttext embeddings (Bojanowski et al., 2017) on a corpus of around 3.1B tokens from scientiﬁc papers which is similar in size to the SciBERT corpus (Beltagy et al., 2019).
items.why: Describes training setup and corpus size for fasttext word embeddings.
items.plain: We trained our own 300-dimensional fasttext word embeddings on a corpus of about 3.1 billion tokens from scientific papers, which is roughly the size of the SciBERT corpus.

items.text: SIF The SIF method of Arora et al. (2017) is a strong text representation baseline that takes a weighted sum of pretrained word vectors (we use fasttext embeddings described above), then computes the ﬁrst principal component of the document embedding matrix and subtracts out each document embedding’s projection to the ﬁrst principal component.
items.why: Explains how the SIF baseline embedding is calculated.
items.plain: The SIF method takes a weighted sum of pretrained fasttext word vectors, calculates the first principal component of the document embedding matrix, and subtracts each document embedding's projection onto that first principal component.

items.text: Citeomatic representations are an L2 normalized weighted sum of title and abstract embeddings, which are trained on the citation graph with dynamic negative sampling.
items.why: Explains the architecture and training setup of the Citeomatic baseline.
items.plain: Citeomatic representations are 75-dimensional, L2-normalized weighted sums of title and abstract embeddings, trained on the citation graph using dynamic negative sampling.

items.text: Following Hamilton et al. (2017a), we used SIF features as node representations, and applied SGC with a range of parameter k, which is the number of times the normalized adjacency is multiplied by the SIF feature matrix.
items.why: Details the experimental setup for the SGC baseline using SIF features.
items.plain: We used SIF features as node representations and applied SGC across different values of k, which controls how many times the normalized adjacency matrix is multiplied by the SIF feature matrix.

items.text: SciBERT To isolate the advantage of SPECTER’s citation-based ﬁne-tuning objective, we add a controlled comparison with SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019).
items.why: States the goal of comparing SPECTER directly against SciBERT.
items.plain: We compare against SciBERT in a controlled setup to isolate the effect of SPECTER's citation-based fine-tuning objective.

items.text: Following Devlin et al. (2019) we take the last layer hidden state corresponding to the [CLS] token as the aggregate document representation.17
items.why: Defines how document representations are extracted from SciBERT.
items.plain: We take the final hidden state of the [CLS] token as the full document representation.

items.text: The model is designed to encode sentences as opposed to paragraphs, so we embed the title and each sentence in the abstract separately, sum the embeddings, and L2 normalize the result to produce a ﬁnal 768-dimensional paper embedding.18
items.why: Describes how sentence-level embeddings are adapted to full paper documents.
items.plain: Because Sentence BERT targets sentences, we embed the title and each abstract sentence separately, sum their vectors, and L2-normalize the result to form a 768-dimensional paper vector.
